source_document.body:
Expeditors International is moving into a new logistics galaxy. The Seattle-based third-party logistics provider announced Wednesday that it will handle logistics for a start-up project designed to support spacecraft launches at Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
Expeditors ( NYSE: EXPD ) will be the exclusive logistics provider and anchor tenant for All Points Logistics LLC, a Florida-based company technical services contractor for the government and defense industry that is developing multi-user spacecraft processing and logistics facilities at Cape Canaveral and Vandenberg Air Force Base in California, to provide cleanroom processing, fueling, storage and other support services to commercial and government launch customers.
Under the long-term lease agreement, Expeditors will provide warehousing, inventory control, inbound transportation management, project cargo services, customs brokerage, supply chain visibility and distribution services for space system operators and manufacturers. The company is also expected to provide similar services in California.
In April, All Points signed an exclusive agreement with NASA for a 65-acre, 50-year lease at Kennedy Space Center to build two facilities. All Points Logistics said it plans to build a 266,000-square foot Spaceport Logistics Center on a 65-acre site at Kennedy Space Center. The facility will be located within five miles of the launch pads and is scheduled to open by the end of 2027. The site will also include an adjacent 260,000 square-foot processing center, integrating launch-site logistics and specialized spacecraft processing capabilities.
U.S. Space Force Command in July awarded All Points a $250 million contract to design and build a commercially owned Spacecraft Processing Center at Vandenberg Space Force Base.
The work is being done by All Points’ Space Prep business, which was created to develop and operate facilities payload processing, storage and other mission support for the space launch industry.
Customers will also have access to Expeditors’ broader global network, connecting suppliers and manufacturing locations with launch operations. The Kennedy Space Center location positions Expeditors to serve existing customers, including hyperscalers, as they explore opportunities in space-based data centers and advanced computing infrastructure, the company said.
“Companies in the space industry manage highly specialized equipment and materials across global supply chains,” said Ed Rone, Expeditors’ regional vice president, U.S. Southeast, in a news release. “This partnership puts our people and services closer to their launch operations, transforming logistics from a transportation function into a mission-readiness capability that helps ensure critical flight hardware, launch equipment, and operational assets are available at the right time.”
Expeditors already has a specialized line of business centered on the aerospace industry. Last summer it expanded its Aircraft on Ground service offering, which helps airlines and suppliers quickly arrange transportation for engines and other critical parts needed for aircraft repairs and maintenance.
The asset-light company had revenue of $4.1 billion during the third quarter, up 41% year over year. Operating income increased 54% to $445.4 million, with management citing high demand from AI-related companies for helping increase revenue.
All Points says that by combining private capital with targeted government investment, it will deliver scalable Infrastructure-as-a-Service capability that provides a more flexible path to more spacecraft processing capacity.
“As an independent provider unaffiliated with launch service providers or spacecraft manufacturers, we offer priority access to the Space Force, [NASA] and neutral access to others with consistent pricing,” said Kevin Brown, senior vice president at Space Prep, in a July 29 news release. “The commercial ownership and operation model frees the government from relying on scarce military construction funding while adding competition and dissimilar redundancy to the nation’s space launch industrial base.”
